Intelligent Agents and Their Environments

Agent Designs and Task Environments

The one idea the whole course is built on: something that perceives, decides, and acts.

In this course, every problem is an agent inside an environment. Once you can say "this is what the agent perceives, this is what it can do, and this is how we measure success", you can choose the right technique for the job. This module gives you that vocabulary, and you will use it in every module after it.

Learning objectives

  • Define an agent, its percepts, and its agent function.
  • Explain rationality, and why it depends on the performance measure and not on luck.
  • Describe a task using PEAS.
  • Classify a task environment along six properties, and say why each one matters.
  • Compare the five agent designs and choose one for a given task.

Key terms in this module

Agent
A system that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon it through actuators. Same definition as Module 1, now with the machinery named.
Percept
What the agent perceives from its environment at one moment — a camera frame, a temperature reading, a click.
Percept sequence
Everything the agent has perceived since it was switched on.
Agent function
The rule that maps any percept sequence to an action. It is the description of behaviour, on paper.
Agent program
The actual code that runs inside the machine and produces that behaviour.
Sensor
The channel through which the agent perceives its environment: a camera, a thermometer, a microphone — or, for a software agent, the chat input that receives messages or the interface that reads a database. The sensor is the channel, not the information it brings in: the camera is the sensor, the image is the percept.
Action
What the agent does to its environment through its actuators: opening a valve, turning a wheel, sending a message, booking a room.
Actuator say: AK-choo-ay-tor
The channel that carries out an action: a motor, a valve, a screen — or, for a software agent, the chat window that sends a reply or the interface that writes to a database or calls an API. The actuator is the channel, not the action itself.
Rational agent
An agent that chooses, for each percept sequence, the action expected to maximize its performance measure, given what it has perceived and what it knows. Rational does not mean perfect or always successful.
Autonomy
How far an agent relies on its own percepts and experience, rather than only on the knowledge its designer built in. Learning is what makes it possible.
Performance measure
How the agent's success is evaluated. It is rarely a single number: some parts are hard requirements, some are things to improve, and some pull against each other. An agent built to maximize it will optimize exactly what you write.
Hard requirement
A rule that must always be true. A solution that breaks it is not accepted, however good it is in other ways. Example: no student has two exams at the same time. Compare with a thing to improve: the fewer rooms, the better. Module 6 calls these hard constraints.
Thing to improve
A part of P where more (or less) is better, but no exact value is required. Example: exams spread as evenly as possible.
Environment
The same idea as in Module 1 — what lies outside the agent and can affect it or be affected by its actions.
PEAS
The four-part checklist for describing an agent's task environment: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.
Task environment
The whole PEAS description of a task — the performance measure, the environment, the actuators and the sensors taken together. The environment alone is one of its four parts.
Fully observable
The agent can perceive, at each step, everything it needs to make a decision. Otherwise the environment is partially observable.
Deterministic say: de-TER-min-istic
The next state is decided completely by the current state and the action. Otherwise it is stochastic (has randomness).
Episodic say: eppi-SOD-ic
Each decision stands alone and does not affect the next one. Otherwise the task is sequential.
Static
The environment does not change while the agent is deciding. Otherwise it is dynamic. If the world waits but your score does not — as in chess with a clock — it is semi-dynamic.
Discrete
States and actions come in countable steps, as in chess. Otherwise the environment is continuous, as with steering angle and speed.
Single-agent
No other agent's actions affect what happens. Otherwise it is multi-agent, and the other agents may cooperate, compete, or both — as other drivers do in traffic.
Condition–action rule
A rule that links a situation to an action: if the soil is dry, then open the valve.
Simple reflex agent
Selects an action from the current percept only, using condition–action rules.
Model-based reflex agent
Keeps an internal state — a picture of the parts of the world it cannot perceive right now — and uses it with condition–action rules.
Goal-based agent
Chooses actions by asking which ones lead towards a goal. This is where search and planning become useful.
Utility-based agent say: yoo-TIL-ity
Uses a utility function to compare outcomes, so it can weigh goals against each other and trade them off.
Utility function
A function that assigns values to outcomes so the agent can compare them. It should agree with the performance measure, but it is not the same thing. Under uncertainty, the agent chooses the action with the best expected utility.
Learning agent
Improves its own behaviour over time from experience and feedback. Learning is not a separate way of selecting actions: it can be added to any of the other designs.
Agentic AI
A commonly used modern term, not a sixth agent design: AI systems that pursue goals with little step-by-step human direction — deciding steps, using tools, observing results, and deciding again. The LLM-based agent of Module 1 is one example.
Section 2.1

What exactly is an agent?

You met this word in Module 1: an agent perceives its environment and acts upon it. That was the idea. This module makes it precise enough to build with — and adds the vocabulary you will use for the rest of the course.

An agent is a system that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon it through actuators. One input at one moment is a percept. Everything it has perceived so far is the percept sequence.

A smart irrigation controller on a farm in Al-Kharj

Sensors: soil moisture probes, a temperature sensor, a weather-forecast feed. Actuators: the valves that open and close each irrigation line. Percept: "soil at line 3 is at 18% moisture, air is 41 degrees." Action: "open valve 3 for twelve minutes."

The farmer is also an agent in the same environment, with eyes as sensors and hands as actuators.

Perceive, then act — again and again. An intelligent agent also decides in between.
i
Decide or act?

Deciding is choosing one option from several: which driver gets the order, which road to take. Acting is doing what was chosen: sending the order, turning the wheel.

Every agent acts. Only an intelligent agent decides — and it decides towards a goal.

Quick test: “decide” answers which one? — “act” answers what did it do?

Function on paper, program in the machine

Agent function

The behaviour

  • A mapping: percept sequence → action
  • A mathematical description, possibly an infinite table
  • Says what the agent does
  • Used when we reason about the agent
Agent program

The implementation

  • Real code, running on real hardware
  • Must fit in memory and answer in time
  • Says how the behaviour is produced
  • Used when we build the agent

Why keep them separate? Because the same behaviour can be produced by very different programs. A lookup table and a clever algorithm may act identically, while one needs a warehouse of memory and the other fits on a small chip.

!
Not every function is an agent function

A spreadsheet formula such as AVERAGE() also maps inputs to an output, but that does not make it an agent function. Here, the inputs are percepts from an environment, and the outputs are actions of an agent in that environment.

6 min read

Section 2.2

Rational does not mean perfect

Students often think a rational agent is one that always gets a good result. That is not the definition, and the difference matters.

A rational agent chooses, for each percept sequence, the action that is expected to maximize its performance measure, given what it has perceived and what it knows.

Crossing the street

You look both ways, see nothing coming, and cross. A piece of metal falls from a passing plane and hits you. Were you irrational?

No. You made the best decision available from what you could perceive. Rationality is judged on the decision, not on the luck. Expecting an agent to be right every time is expecting it to be all-knowing, which no agent is.

The performance measure is a design decision — yours

The performance measure is set by the designer, not by the agent. Judge the agent by what counts as success for the people who will use it.

!
The classic trap

Reward a cleaning robot for the amount of dust collected, and a clever agent learns to dump the dust back on the floor and collect it again. It scores brilliantly and cleans nothing. The agent did not cheat: it optimized exactly what you wrote. Measure the clean floor, not the dust collected. This is the lesson of section 1.6: a system pursues the objective it was given, not the one you had in mind.

Four things rationality depends on

The performance measure; the agent's built-in knowledge of the environment; the actions it can take; and its percept sequence so far. Change any one of them and the rational action can change. This is why "is this agent rational?" is never answerable until you state all four.

Learning and autonomy

An agent that only follows what its designer wrote is not autonomous — it relies on the designer's knowledge of the world. An agent that learns from its own experience can correct wrong assumptions and survive changes the designer never imagined. A practical system usually starts with built-in knowledge (so it is not useless on day one) and learns after that.

Check yourself

Two food delivery agents work in Riyadh. Agent A is judged on "orders delivered per hour". Agent B is judged on "orders delivered on time, with the food still hot, and no traffic violations". Which behaviours will you see from each?

Show answer

Agent A will take risks: speeding, accepting too many orders at once, choosing the shortest route regardless of safety, and dropping the food quickly at the door. Every one of those raises orders per hour. Agent B has a measure closer to what the customer actually wants, so it will refuse orders it cannot serve well. Same environment, same actions available — the measure produced the behaviour.

Section 2.3

PEAS: describing an agent's task environment

Before designing an agent, we need to describe the task it will perform and the environment in which it will operate.

PEAS is a framework for describing an agent's task environment. It helps us specify what counts as success, what the agent is dealing with, how it can act, and how it perceives.

PEAS stands for:

P — Performance measure: how the agent's success is evaluated.

E — Environment: what lies outside the agent and can affect it or be affected by its actions.

A — Actuators: how the agent acts on its environment.

S — Sensors: how the agent perceives its environment.

A note about “environment”. You met it in Module 1, and the E line above is the same idea, now written as part of the agent's task. The complete description — P + E + A + S — is what we call the agent's task environment.

Task environment = P + E + A + S

Environment = E only

You have already seen two of the four: the irrigation controller in section 2.1 listed its sensors and its actuators. PEAS adds the P and the E, and turns the description into a standard four-line form.

Example: a self-driving taxi in Riyadh

Notice how many things sit in P. A real performance measure is rarely one number.

Two more, quickly

  1. An exam timetabling agent at the university

    P: zero student clashes and no room over capacity — these are hard requirements, not preferences; then exams spread as evenly as possible across the period. E: the courses, the students, the rooms, the exam period, the registration database, and the exam timetable system. A: timetable system — writes each exam into a room and a time slot. S: database interface — reads student enrolments from the registration database.

  2. An Arabic customer-service assistant

    P: questions answered correctly from the knowledge base, in as few turns as possible. Escalating to a human when unsure counts as a correct answer, not a failure — and a confident wrong answer is the most expensive outcome of all. E: the customer, the company's knowledge base, the account system, and the ticket system. A: chat window — sends replies; ticket system — opens a ticket; transfer — passes the chat to a human staff member. S: chat input — reads the customer's messages; account interface — reads the account history; knowledge-base search — reads the matching answers.

Notice that the parts of a P are not all the same kind. Some are hard requirements (rules that must always be true) — no student sitting two exams at once. Others are things to improve as far as possible — the fewest rooms, the shortest trip. And some pull against each other: a faster trip is a less comfortable one. Section 2.5 shows how a utility-based agent weighs the ones that pull against each other.

One more rule — easy to state, and easy to break. Write P in terms of what counts as success — the outcome you want — not in terms of how you imagine the agent should behave. “The floor is clean” is an outcome. “The robot moves in a spiral pattern” is a guess at a method — and if you write it into the measure, a spiral is exactly what you will get, clean floor or not.

Robot or software: where do things go?

Ask one question for each letter. The answer tells you where an item goes.

PEASAskWrite it as
PHow do we measure success?something you can count: hard requirements first, then things to improve
EWhat is outside the agent, affecting it or affected by it?things: the customer, the road, the database
AHow does the agent act on its environment?channel — what it does
SHow does the agent get information?channel — what it reads

Information comes in through S. Action goes out through A. A sensor is the channel, not the information: the camera is the sensor, and the image is the percept. In the same way, an actuator is the channel, not the action.

Self-driving taxi (robot)Customer-service assistant (software)
Scameras, radar, GPSchat input — reads the customer's messages; account interface — reads the account history
Asteering, brakes, screenchat window — sends replies; ticket system — opens a ticket

For a robot, S and A are physical parts. For a software agent, they are channels: S reads (messages, files, database records) and A writes or sends (a reply, a database row, an API call).

The same system can appear in three places. In E it is a thing: the exam timetable system. In S it is read: timetable system — reads change requests. In A it is changed: timetable system — writes each exam into a slot. That is correct, not a mistake.

Some agents are software but use physical parts, such as a smart car-park guide that reads fixed cameras and lights up signs. Place each part by what it does, not by what kind of agent it is.

More practice: PEAS Made Simple has four worked examples, eight self-check questions, and short notes in Arabic.

PEAS is where projects are won or lost

A perfect algorithm cannot rescue a wrong PEAS. A performance measure that rewards the wrong thing, or sensors that cannot perceive what the decision actually needs, will defeat any algorithm you put behind them. Write the PEAS before you write any code — and show it to the person who asked for the system, because they will correct the P immediately.

6 min read

Section 2.4

Six properties of a task environment

What kind of world is my agent operating in? PEAS gave us a description of the agent's task environment. Now we classify that task environment along six properties.

Some of these properties depend on the agent itself — especially what its sensors allow it to perceive — not only on the world around it. That is why we call them properties of the task environment, not just of the Environment (E) in PEAS.

These properties help determine which AI techniques are suitable for the task. Ask six questions about every task.

  1. Fully or partially observable?

    Can the agent perceive everything it needs to make a decision? A chess board is fully observable. A taxi is partially observable — it cannot know everything about the road, or what another driver intends to do.

  2. Deterministic or stochastic?

    Does the same action in the same state always give the same result? Moving a chess piece, yes. Braking on a wet road, not necessarily.

  3. Episodic or sequential?

    Does this decision affect the next ones? Sorting parcels by their labels is episodic — each parcel can be handled on its own. Driving is sequential: what you do now changes the choices available later.

  4. Static or dynamic?

    Does the environment change while the agent is deciding? A crossword waits for you. Traffic does not. In a dynamic environment, taking too long to decide can make a good answer useless. There is also a middle case, semi-dynamic: the world waits, but your score does not. In chess with a clock, the board stays still while you think, yet every second you spend is counted against you.

  5. Discrete or continuous?

    Are the states and actions separate, countable choices, or do they vary over a continuous range? Chess is discrete. Steering angle and speed are continuous.

  6. Single-agent or multi-agent?

    Are there other agents whose actions affect what happens? Are they cooperating, competing, or both? Driving is multi-agent: other drivers affect what your agent should do. Competitive multi-agent environments lead us to adversarial search, which we study in Module 5.

Swipe sideways to see all six properties →

TaskObservableDeterministicEpisodicStaticDiscreteAgents
Crossword puzzleFullyDeterministicSequentialStaticDiscreteSingle
Chess with a clockFullyDeterministicSequentialSemi-dynamicDiscreteMulti
Exam timetablingFullyDeterministicSequentialStaticDiscreteSingle

Driving in RiyadhPartiallyStochasticSequentialDynamicContinuousMulti
These properties do not just describe the task — they help us choose how to solve it.
Why these six questions matter

These properties are not just labels. They help us decide how an agent should solve its task.

When the task environment is fully observable, deterministic, static, discrete and single-agent, the agent can perceive what matters and predict the result of each action, so it can plan a whole solution before it acts. That is the setting of Module 3. Change a property and the problem changes with it. Some problems involve continuous variables; when the goal is to optimize a differentiable objective (one whose slope we can compute), methods such as gradient descent (Module 4) may be useful. An opponent calls for the adversarial search of Module 5. Chance in a game, such as dice, returns in Module 5. Missing information needs tools that go beyond this course.

That is why we describe the task environment before choosing an AI technique.

7 min read

Section 2.5

Five agent designs

All agents receive percepts and produce actions. What differs is how they select those actions. Some react directly, some remember what has happened, some plan towards goals, some compare possible outcomes, and some can learn from experience. In the language of section 2.1, these are five ways to write the agent program.

1. Simple reflex agent

Looks at the current percept only, and matches it against condition–action rules: if soil is dry, then open the valve.

Good: tiny, fast, easy to test. Bad: blind to anything it cannot perceive right now. If the moisture sensor breaks and reads "dry" forever, the agent floods the field and never notices. It works well only when the current percept is enough to select the right action — for example, in a fully observable environment.

2. Model-based reflex agent

Keeps an internal state: a picture of the parts of the world it cannot currently perceive, updated with each percept and with knowledge of how the world changes. This is how an agent copes with a partially observable environment.

Our irrigation agent now remembers that line 3 was watered twenty minutes ago, so a "dry" reading is suspicious. That internal state, together with its knowledge of how the world changes and how its own actions change it, is its model.

3. Goal-based agent

Knows what it is trying to achieve, and asks which action sequence leads there. This is where search and planning become useful — Module 3 studies search in detail.

A reflex taxi turns right because the rule says so. A goal-based taxi turns right because it has worked out that this road leads to the passenger's destination. Give it a new destination and it plans a new route, with no new rules written.

4. Utility-based agent

A goal tells the agent what it wants to achieve, but it may not tell it which of several successful outcomes is better. A utility function gives outcomes values, allowing the agent to compare them and trade one thing against another: faster but less comfortable, cheaper but slower, safer but longer.

It also handles uncertainty: when an action might succeed or fail, the agent can choose the one with the best expected utility.

The utility function is the agent's own, internal version of the performance measure. The designer judges the agent by the performance measure; the agent uses its utility function to choose. When the two agree, choosing the highest expected utility is rational.

5. Learning agent

A learning agent improves its behaviour from experience. Learning is not a completely separate way of selecting actions: it can be added to the designs above.

For example, a goal-based route planner may learn from previous journeys and improve its estimates of travel time. It still plans towards a goal, but now its behaviour can improve with experience.

Choose the simplest design that solves your problem — not the most advanced one.
i
Start with the simplest design that works

If a reflex rule solves the job, use the reflex rule. A learning agent that needs thousands of examples, careful monitoring, and a retraining plan is a bad answer to a problem that two if statements solve correctly. Engineering judgement means matching the design to the environment, not showing off.

i
How this connects to Module 1

In Module 1, we used a simple introductory distinction: an agent perceives and acts, while an intelligent agent perceives, decides, and acts towards a goal. The five designs here answer a different question: how is the action selected? Simple and model-based reflex agents mainly follow condition–action rules. Goal-based and utility-based agents explicitly evaluate actions in relation to goals or preferences. A learning agent can improve the way any of these designs behaves.

Rationality is a separate idea: it asks how well an agent selects its actions according to its performance measure. In a simple enough environment, even a simple reflex agent can be rational.

!
A word you will hear: agentic AI

Outside this course you will often hear systems described as agentic AI. Agentic AI is not a sixth agent design. The term is commonly used today for AI systems that can pursue goals with little step-by-step human direction — deciding steps, using tools, observing results, and deciding what to do next. One example is the LLM-based agent from Module 1: a large language model (LLM) does the perceiving and the reasoning, and tools act as its actuators (search, files, other software, an API).

So judge one exactly as you judge any agent in this module. What is its performance measure? What can it actually perceive? What can it actually do? How does it select actions — does it use goals, a model, utility, learning, or some combination of them? The label is recent and used loosely in industry; those questions are not.

Check yourself

A robot vacuum in a flat in Jeddah. What is the simplest design each behaviour needs? (a) "If I hit a wall, turn." (b) "Do not clean the kitchen twice before cleaning the bedroom." (c) "Finish before the family comes home, but stay quiet during nap time."

Show answer

(a) Simple reflex — it uses only the current percept. (b) Model-based — it must remember which rooms it already cleaned, which it cannot perceive right now. (c) Utility-based — finishing on time and staying quiet are competing preferences. The agent needs a way to compare the value of different outcomes and choose the best trade-off.

Revision card

Module 2 cheat sheet

Core definitions

  • Agent = perceives through sensors, acts through actuators
  • Environment = what lies outside the agent and can affect it or be affected by its actions
  • Percept = one input · percept sequence = everything perceived so far
  • Agent function = percept sequence → action (on paper)
  • Agent program = the code that produces it (in the machine)

Rationality — three terms not to mix

  • Performance measure = how the agent's success is evaluated — it defines success
  • Utility function = assigns values to outcomes so the agent can compare them — it helps the agent choose
  • Rational action = the action expected to maximize the performance measure, given what the agent has perceived and knows
  • Judged on the decision, not on the luck of the outcome
  • Depends on four things: the measure, built-in knowledge, available actions, percepts so far
  • Rational ≠ all-knowing, and rational ≠ perfect
  • Autonomous = relies on its own experience, not only on what the designer built in

PEAS

  • Performance measure · Environment · Actuators · Sensors
  • Task environment = P + E + A + S · Environment = E only
  • S = information IN · A = action OUT · write each as channel — what it does; the sensor is the channel, not the information
  • P usually has several parts: hard requirements (they must always be true), things to improve, and parts that pull against each other (e.g. safety, time, cost)
  • P describes what counts as success, not how the agent achieves it
  • Write PEAS before writing code

Six properties of a task environment

  • Properties of the task environment, not of E alone — observability depends on the sensors
  • Fully / partially observable — can the agent perceive everything it needs?
  • Deterministic / stochastic — same action, same state, always the same result?
  • Episodic / sequential — does this decision affect the next ones?
  • Static / dynamic — does the world change while the agent decides? (semi-dynamic: the world waits, but your score does not — as in chess with a clock)
  • Discrete / continuous — countable choices, or a continuous range?
  • Single-agent / multi-agent — do other agents' actions matter? cooperating, competing, or both
  • Module 3 search assumes: fully observable, deterministic, static, discrete, single-agent — and sequential, because a plan is a sequence of actions
  • Continuous variables + a differentiable objective → e.g. gradient descent (Module 4) · an opponent → Module 5

Five agent designs — react → remember → plan → compare → learn

  • Simple reflex — current percept only; works when that percept is enough (fully observable)
  • Model-based reflex — maintains an internal state of aspects of the world it cannot currently perceive (partially observable)
  • Goal-based — plans towards a goal → search and planning become useful
  • Utility-based — uses utility to compare outcomes and choose among alternatives
  • Learning — improves itself from experience; can be added to any of the four
  • Agentic AI — a commonly used modern term, not a sixth agent design: AI systems that pursue goals with little step-by-step human direction, often by planning steps and using tools

Mistakes that cost marks

  • Saying an agent was irrational because the outcome was bad
  • Confusing the performance measure with the agent's internal decision mechanism — the measure defines success; it does not tell the agent how to act
  • Mixing up agent function (behaviour) and agent program (code)
  • Treating the six properties as properties of E alone
  • Calling chess with a clock "dynamic" — it is semi-dynamic
  • Calling learning the fifth, "smartest" design — it can improve any design
  • Saying a simple reflex agent can never be rational
  • Choosing a learning agent when two if statements would do the job
